chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
title: Leading the band on tour in 1944: Bird and a bandmate beaten by Mississippi police
summary: On the way to California with McShann gone, police at Natchez beat Bird and another man; Ramey recalls Bird talking them out of trouble elsewhere.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: First of all, when McShann first -- well, when he had to leave we played the Howard Theatre in Washington, and this was in January of '44, and we had -- the band was booked

in the Plantation Club in California. When McShann had to leave for his pre-induction thing, whatever that was, and so he put the band in my charge and I took the band on one-nighters all the way across -- that's when -- the story -- when I told the story about Bird getting beat up by the cops in Jackson, Mississippi? You didn't hear that?

We played at a -- it was a new dance hall right on the river. And there was a curfew for blacks. Had to be in the house with the lights out by 11:00. And now, it was down at this place -- everybody was still talking about that place where somebody set that dance hall on fire and burned up all those musicians.
Natchez.

Natchez, Mississippi. Now, this was right on the river, like that. We had two valets, so we got there and got the instructions, and I told all the guys. I said, well, we're going to put one of you on the door to check the take, and we want another guy to stand outside and watch for anybody that's coming, because this was a brand-new, unpainted dance hall, right on the river, there.

And so we want you to watch them because we know how mean these people are in Mississippi. So they said -- it was quite a few white guys that you could see standing back there, but nothing ever happened. We played the thing, we
got through, we got home, we got into bed and turned out the lights, all of us except Walter Brown and Bird.

Now, they didn't have a light on the front porch where they slept. This was a rooming house. And so naturally all of us in the band filled that house up and so Bird and what's his name -- the lady gave them a bed on the front porch. Now, I don't know whether they were smoking pot or cigarettes. Evidently they must have been smoking cigarettes because if it had been pot they probably would have been in jail forever.

But, anyway, from what we got -- I had to call Johnny Tuning and he had to come and get Bird out, we didn't know where Bird was. Til finally the lady came, the lady that owned the place, and she stayed next door because we had taken her bedroom, too. And she said, the cops came last night and took two of your boys away.

And so we found out that the cops had said that the guys had a light on the front porch. They were supposed to have been laying in bed, smoking cigarettes. Because it was a screened porch. So they took Bird and what's his name. We got them two days later. I was in Little Rock, Arkansas. We had played Memphis and Nashville, the band was in Little Rock when they caught up with us. Johnny had to go get them and bring them to catch up with us.
And Bird -- and they had knots on their head big enough to hang a hat on.
Had beaten them up?
Oh, they really had a beating. And so I carried the band on to --
Why in the hell would they do that? Or do you think Bird sort of sassed them?

No, no, you didn't have to do anything. In fact, Bird was gifted, he got us out of trouble many a time. I remember one time, we were on our way to New Orleans and we got just past -- gotten just through Baton Rouge, and the cops caught us and said, 'You Yankee niggers, huh?' And Bird got up and no, sir, yes, sir and everything, turned him out nice and his clothes fit on him, and how his father worked down here in Louisiana. His father had never even been there. And after all he said, they actually escorted us to the next town.

Bird was talented at that. I'm pretty sure it wasn't that. It just was some people to use as examples, like, in Texas they used to do that back in the -- when we were kids, get some guy and lynch him and drag him through the black neighborhood or something.
Oh, yeah.
Tar him or something, put something on him and drag him through the neighborhood, as an example to put fear in the rest of the --
Just to keep them frightened.
Keep frightened, yeah. So I think it
